name: Skin whitening/bleaching

image.caption: Sweet Georgia Brown skin bleaching cream advertisement 1930s

lead: Skin whitening, also called lightening or bleaching, uses chemical agents to reduce melanin so skin looks lighter and more even. People use it to fade dark spots, brighten the complexion and lift overall tone, and some looksmaxxing posters say it raises their rating by roughly 0.5 to 1 PSL.

Most lightening agents inhibit tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production; others block melanin transfer to skin cells or destroy melanocytes. Glutathione is reported to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin toward its lighter form. Agents such as hydroquinone, arbutin and kojic acid have been studied for pigmentation disorders, and the practice itself dates back more than two thousand years.

paras: People use topical creams and serums, oral supplements, or clinic-administered injections, usually as a routine over weeks to months, often alongside sunscreen and general skincare. Results show gradually as existing pigment fades and new pigment production is reduced.

Reported harms include mercury toxicity from contaminated products, skin thinning from long-term steroid creams, ochronosis and contact dermatitis from hydroquinone, and serious reactions from intravenous glutathione. Skin becomes more sun-sensitive. Many products are restricted or banned in several countries, and regulators and dermatology reviews document these problems.

angle.text: Users apply or take lightening agents to reduce melanin, fading dark spots and lifting overall skin tone for a brighter, more even complexion. Some forum posters say it raises their rating by about 0.5 to 1 PSL. Topical agents such as hydroquinone and arbutin have been studied clinically for pigmentation.

lead: Skin whitening, also called skin lightening or skin bleaching, is the use of chemical substances to lighten skin color or even out tone by reducing the amount of melanin in the skin. Within looksmaxxing it is discussed as a way to change complexion toward a lighter, more even or differently toned look, sometimes labelled "whitemaxxing", and some forum users say it raises their appearance ratings. [1][2]

The practice is far older than the internet. Wikipedia traces recorded lightening efforts back more than two thousand years and across Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas, with usage figures such as 77% of Nigerian women, 52% of Senegalese women and 25% of Malian women reported for 2013, and over 50% of skin-care sales in India attributed to lightening formulations. [1] A 2022 dermatology review describes cosmetic skin lightening as a growing public health issue among communities of color, with documented adverse effects alongside social and cultural drivers. [3]

Agents in use include hydroquinone, kojic acid, azelaic acid, retinoids, topical corticosteroids, oral or intravenous glutathione, tranexamic acid, chemical peels, lasers and, illicitly, mercury compounds. Their mechanisms centre on tyrosinase, the key enzyme of melanin production. [1][4][5] Research covers individual agents, mostly for pigmentation disorders such as melasma, and reviews of glutathione describe a gap between popularity and trial evidence. [6]

paras: Skin color is determined largely by the amount and type of melanin produced by melanocytes and transferred to surrounding skin cells. Lightening products aim to reduce that pigment or the signals that produce it. Wikipedia lists six broad mechanisms: inhibiting tyrosinase activity, reducing tyrosinase expression or activation (including downregulation of the transcription factor MITF), scavenging intermediates of melanin synthesis, blocking transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes, directly breaking down existing melanin, and destroying melanocytes, as is done in some vitiligo treatment. [1] A medicinal chemistry review describes tyrosinase inhibitors as the main route of drug development, and a 2011 review of melanogenesis covers both established and newer approaches. [4][5]

Grokipedia states that skin color is largely genetically determined and that no method permanently changes base skin tone; it presents the topical and procedural options as reducing pigment for as long as they are used. [7]

Hydroquinone decreases melanin production and is described by Wikipedia as a common and effective agent for hyperpigmentation; its lightening effect was first reported in 1936. [1][8] Kojic acid, derived from fungi, inhibits tyrosinase in a slow-binding manner in laboratory work and is permitted in European cosmetics. [9][1] Tretinoin, a retinoid, is used for specific areas and sometimes in combination with steroids and hydroquinone. Alpha hydroxy acids exfoliate the surface, with side effects that include sun sensitivity and irritation. Azelaic acid is described as a possible second-line option for melasma, and a 2017 review found tentative evidence for tranexamic acid in melasma while another found evidence insufficient. [1]

Glutathione, an antioxidant the body produces, is the agent most often taken by mouth for lightening and is also used in creams and, in some places, by injection. [1] Natural and plant-derived tyrosinase inhibitors, including compounds from mulberry and licorice such as oxyresveratrol and glabridin, have been studied in the laboratory and are used in cosmetic products. [10][11][12][13] Procedures such as laser treatment have been used for melasma, with Wikipedia noting recurrence is common and that some lasers can increase pigmentation. [1]

Corticosteroids such as clobetasol propionate are among the most commonly incorporated agents in lightening creams sold informally, and inorganic mercury has historically been the active ingredient in many products. [1]

Wikipedia reports records of lightening practice from over 200 B.C., with honey and olive oil in Egypt and Greece, rice powder in Edo-period Japan, powdered pearl in China, and white lead and mercury preparations in Greece, Rome and Elizabethan Europe, where lead-and-vinegar ceruse was associated with lead poisoning. In the United States it describes arsenic complexion wafers advertised in 1889 and products marketed to Black American women from the mid-19th century. [1]

Regionally, the article describes light skin as associated with wealth and separation from outdoor labor in East and South Asia, with colonial hierarchies and film industries reinforcing the association, and with Latin American blanqueamiento ideology. It reports that South Africa began regulating mercury and high-hydroquinone products in the 1970s, that light-skin preferences in Ghana are documented from the 16th century, and that use rose in several African countries after independence movements. [1] In 1997 French police dismantled a trafficking network in lightening products, and a Paris hospital later opened a department for resulting skin disorders. [1]

Scholars cited by Wikipedia link the practice to colorism and to perceived social mobility, including studies connecting lighter skin to marriage prospects and income, while a representative of an Indian product line is quoted as saying such products enabled socioeconomic mobility comparable to education. [1] Grokipedia takes a different framing, saying colonial-origin narratives are exaggerated and that preferences predate colonialism. [7] A 2022 review frames the practice as having sociocultural implications that clinicians should discuss sensitively with patients. [3]

Wikipedia reports that over 25% of women in a number of African countries and about 40% in Asia regularly use lightening products, that women use them more than men in Africa, and that a 2013 projection put the global market at US$19.8 billion by 2018. [1] Grokipedia cites a pooled lifetime rate of 27.7% and gives market estimates between roughly US$8 billion and US$12 billion in the early 2020s; its figures vary between sections. [7] Reporting in Der Spiegel in 2020, cited by Wikipedia, described pressure in Ghana linking lighter skin to earnings, including mothers applying lotion to infants. [1]

Evidence differs by agent. A 2016 review of glutathione as a skin-lightening agent described a dichotomy between popularity and evidence, reported no evidence supporting intravenous efficacy, and noted that adverse effects led the Philippine FDA to issue warnings. [6] A 2025 narrative review reported significant but variable melanin reductions with oral glutathione and good-level reductions with topical forms of varying sustainability, while describing intravenous use as linked to serious safety concerns such as anaphylaxis and hepatotoxicity and calling for large, rigorous trials.  Grokipedia describes a 2016 intravenous glutathione trial in which more participants in the treatment group than the placebo group reported lighter skin, with effects fading by about six months, and a 12-week oral trial reporting significant lightening versus placebo; these details come from that page alone. [7]

For hydroquinone, Wikipedia calls it the most effective treatment for hyperpigmentation, with a trial for hyperpigmentation in 1961 and a 1975 trial of a combination with tretinoin and dexamethasone for melasma. [8] Wikipedia states glutathione's effectiveness was unclear as of 2019 and that kojic acid has been reported effective in some studies. [1] A 2011 review notes that existing agents are mainly competitive inhibitors of tyrosinase and are used clinically for melasma, café-au-lait spots and solar lentigo. [5]

Human research consists mainly of trials and reviews of individual agents, chiefly hydroquinone and glutathione, studied for melasma and other pigmentation disorders or for skin tone. [6][5][8] No studies found that test whether lightening healthy skin changes attractiveness ratings or dating outcomes, the claim made in looksmaxxing forum threads. [2]

The European Union banned hydroquinone, tretinoin and corticosteroids in cosmetics, with the hydroquinone ban dated to 2000, while kojic acid and low-concentration alpha hydroxy acids remain permitted. [1] Wikipedia's hydroquinone article describes its US status as shifting: classified generally recognized as safe and effective in 1982, approval revoked in 2006 with a proposed over-the-counter ban, and officially banned from over-the-counter use in 2020 under a broader reform of over-the-counter drug rules. [8] South Africa began regulating mercury and high-hydroquinone products in the 1970s. [1]

On mercury, the Minamata Convention was approved in Geneva in January 2013, opened for signature in Kumamoto in October 2013 and entered into force on 16 August 2017; it covers mercury-added soaps and cosmetics, which parties are to prohibit from manufacture, import and export by 2020, subject to exemptions. [14] Wikipedia reports that many mercury, hydroquinone and steroid products are illegal to sell in various countries including the UK but continue to be found, with enforcement often weak. [1]

Wikipedia lists acute pneumonitis and gastric irritation from mercury, long-term kidney and neurological effects including insomnia and memory loss, and skin discoloration as mercury accumulates in the dermis. [1] For hydroquinone it lists ochronosis (blue-black pigment deposition), cataracts, patchy depigmentation and contact dermatitis; the FDA has said it cannot rule out hydroquinone as a potential carcinogen based on absorption and rat tumor data, and the US National Toxicology Program found some evidence of long-term carcinogenic and genotoxic effects. [1][8]

Long-term topical corticosteroids over large areas can cause skin atrophy and fragility, glaucoma, cataracts and other systemic steroid effects, and lightened skin is more susceptible to sun damage and infection. [1] A 2000 Senegal study cited by Wikipedia identified chronic use as a risk factor for hypertension and diabetes. [1] Grokipedia reports a 2020 South African study finding biochemical hypoadrenalism in about a fifth of steroid-cream users and a 2019 US case of methylmercury toxicity from a lightening product. [7] Reviews describe serious adverse events with intravenous glutathione. [6]

Skin lightening appears in looksmax.org threads, usually framed around the PSL rating scale and ethnicity. One thread opens by saying lightening adds half a point to a full point of PSL and lists products and video channels; replies dispute whether lighter skin is desirable. [2] Another poster says injected glutathione is the only lightener that works and dismisses vitamin C, niacinamide, kojic acid and azelaic acid as ineffective, while a reply defends a "skin lightening stack". [15] A user describing an olive, Fitzpatrick type III-IV complexion asks for products for a lighter tone with reddish undertones, and replies list supplements such as glutathione and vitamin C alongside kojic soap, tretinoin and glycolic acid exfoliation. [16] A further thread raises the theory that lightening products used during puberty might lead to darker skin afterwards as melanin production rebounds; it is a hypothesis posted by a user. [17]

Several threads have titles indicating ongoing community interest, including guides and posts about whether a particular user's bleaching changed his look. No published study has evaluated the PSL scale or claimed rating gains from lightening.

lore.intro: Skin lightening is discussed on looksmax.org as a method to change one's rating or ethnic appearance, with debate over which agents work and whether lighter skin is more attractive. [2][15][16]
